As its heavy siblings die they shed most of their mass in winds, shells and explosions, and by this age a cluster has typically lost around a third of its starting mass that way. Less weight means a weaker grip on everyone left, and this family has weathered that slow loss along with the galaxy's tug, so what you see is the remnant of a heavier family.

M39.beat: Thinning out: a family near the end of its cluster days
M39.question: Will M39 still be a cluster a few hundred million years from now?
M39.why: M39 is a nearby family about 430 million years old, close enough to count its brightest members one by one, and it has reached the age at which most families start to come apart.
M39.look: From Deneb sweep about nine degrees east-north-east to a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon. Count the members you can see at low power: they are spread wide, with no tight core.
M39.answer: M39 will probably have dissolved by then: with only about 500 Suns' worth of stars, its gravity is too weak to resist the galaxy's pull for ever. Its members will go on traveling side by side long after the cluster has gone, a family recognizable only by its shared motion.
M39.story: The end of a cluster is a slow unwinding rather than an explosion. Escaped members keep nearly the cluster's orbit around the galaxy, those slightly closer in pulling ahead and those slightly farther out falling behind, so the family stretches into a long thin stream along its path. After a few more laps the stream grows so long and faint that only careful measurements of motion can still trace it.

M3.beat: Thinning out: too heavy ever to scatter
M3.question: Can a star family be heavy enough never to come apart at all?
M3.why: M3 is a star family in a completely different weight class from the open clusters, and an extreme test of how much a family's weight matters.
M3.look: A little past halfway from Cor Caroli toward Arcturus, find an obvious round glow, brighter toward the middle. It will not break into stars in binoculars: its siblings crowd far too closely to separate.
M3.answer: A family can come very close: M3 has kept hundreds of thousands of siblings together for most of the age of the universe. It manages this because its gravity dwarfs anything an open cluster can muster and its orbit keeps it out in the halo, far from the crowded disk where lighter families are torn apart. The Sun's family, like almost every family, was born far lighter.
M3.story: Even a family this heavy leaks. In the crowded core, close passes now and then fling a star out fast enough to escape, and each crossing of the galaxy's disk squeezes the cluster and loosens a few more. So globular clusters slowly shed members too, a few at a time over billions of years. Some lighter ones have already dissolved completely, and their stars, drawn out into long streams, now belong to the galaxy's halo.

M93.beat: Thinning out: a compact old arrowhead
M93.question: How has M93 kept its family close for some 700 million years?
M93.why: M93 is a family in its later years, well past the age at which most clusters lose their shape, yet it still reads as a tight arrowhead.
M93.look: Start at Xi Puppis and move about one and a half degrees north-west to a small, bright, arrowhead-shaped clump, a dozen or so stars resolved over a soft glow. Note how compact it still is.
M93.answer: It was born dense: some 2,500 Suns' worth of stars packed into a clump about 20 light-years across hold on to one another far better than a sprawling family could. It is thinning all the same, but it has kept its shape where lighter families have lost theirs.
M93.story: Astronomers measure a family's compactness by the radius that encloses half of its members. A family with a small half-mass radius keeps most of its stars deep inside the reach of its own gravity, so the galaxy's tide, which acts most strongly on the outskirts, finds few members to pull away. A family born packed into a small, dense clump has kept that advantage all its life, which is why its shape has lasted.

Mel20.beat: First to age: Mirfak, the family's eldest
Mel20.question: Why does Mirfak look yellower than the blue-white siblings around it?
Mel20.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster is a family so near that it fills the whole binocular field, and its brightest member stands apart from its siblings in color as well as in brightness.
Mel20.look: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains across the field. Compare Mirfak's tint with theirs: it is a shade yellower than any of its siblings.
Mel20.answer: Mirfak was born the heaviest of the family, so it burned through its core hydrogen first and swelled into a supergiant, its surface cooling to yellow-white while its lighter siblings stay blue-white in their prime. Born on the same day, they are reading different pages of the same life, and Mirfak is several chapters ahead.
Mel20.story: Mirfak is also a test of how well we understand aging stars. The family's lithium clock and the age implied by Mirfak's own size and temperature do not agree perfectly. Since the family's age is the sturdier figure, the gap points to physics the models have not quite captured, perhaps how heavy stars mix their cores or the spin they were born with. A family whose eldest has already turned is a laboratory for exactly that question.

AST-OrionBelt.question: Will the Belt stars and their young siblings stay together as they age?
AST-OrionBelt.why: Orion's Belt marks the heart of a young family of a different kind from a cluster: hot, heavy siblings spread across several degrees of sky, the brightest family of the winter sky.
AST-OrionBelt.look: Put the middle Belt star at the center and let the outer two sit near the edges. An S-shaped chain of fainter stars winds through the field, and many of them share the Belt stars' blue-white color and their birth.
AST-OrionBelt.answer: These siblings will not stay together. An association like this is born too loose for its own gravity to hold, so they are already drifting apart while only a few million years old. In time they will spread across whole constellations, tied together only by the direction they travel.
AST-OrionBelt.story: That a group like this is flying apart was shown by its motions. In the 1950s Adriaan Blaauw found that the stars of such associations move outward from a common center, like fragments of a slow explosion. Running the motions backward gave the time since they were together, a second clock alongside the ages read from the stars themselves. Gaia has since measured those motions for thousands of members across Orion and found the same pattern, branch by branch.

HR1712.question: How far can a star travel from its family in two and a half million years?
HR1712.why: AE Aurigae looks like an ordinary faint star near M38, but it was born in Orion, and it shows the most dramatic way a family can lose a member.
HR1712.look: From M38 drift about three degrees west-south-west to the lone, brighter star there. Nothing in the view marks it as unusual; its family tie is written entirely in its motion.
HR1712.answer: It can cross a good part of the sky. Flung out of the Orion Nebula's young cluster at high speed, AE Aurigae has covered hundreds of light-years and now shines among the stars of Auriga, far from any sibling. Its partner in flight, μ Columbae, left at the same moment in the opposite direction.
HR1712.story: Stars are thrown out of families in two ways. In one, a heavy partner explodes and its companion, suddenly released, flies off at its orbital speed. In the other, a close encounter among several stars in a crowded young cluster flings one outward while the rest tighten into a closer pair. AE Aurigae is the textbook case of the second kind, because the tightened pair it left behind can still be found in Orion's Sword.

HR1996.question: Where is μ Columbae's partner in flight now?
HR1996.why: μ Columbae is a faint star in the Dove, south of Orion, and the family it came from lies far to the north, in Orion's Sword.
HR1996.look: From Phact, the brightest star of Columba, nudge about two degrees north-east to the faint bluish-white star there. Its color matches the hot young stars of Orion's Sword, the family it left.
HR1996.answer: Its partner is AE Aurigae, on the other side of Orion in Auriga, flung out of the same young cluster in the opposite direction. Two siblings born in one nest now sit on opposite sides of the constellation that made them.
HR1996.story: Tracing μ Columbae home works only because it moves so fast. Like the partner it left with, it flies at around a hundred kilometers a second relative to its surroundings, many times the gentle drift of ordinary stars, so its path stands out clearly against the background. The Hipparcos satellite's precise motions let astronomers run both paths back to a single point and a single moment. Slower escapees from the same nursery have surely left too, but their trails are lost among the drifting stars of Orion.

DS-MizarAlcor.question: Do Mizar and Alcor belong to a bigger family than just each other?
DS-MizarAlcor.why: Mizar and Alcor are the famous pair in the Big Dipper's handle, and they are part of the clearest example of scattered siblings in the northern sky.
DS-MizarAlcor.look: Center the middle star of the Dipper's handle with Alcor beside it, then sweep along the handle and across the bowl. Mizar, Alioth, Megrez, Phecda and Merak share one white color, while Dubhe at the bowl's far corner is yellow-orange.
DS-MizarAlcor.answer: They belong to a much bigger family. The pair moves through space in step with Merak, Phecda, Megrez and Alioth, all born together about 414 million years ago. That family has since spread over some twenty degrees of sky, and only its shared motion still marks them as kin.
DS-MizarAlcor.story: The Dipper's family reaches far beyond the Dipper. Stars that share its motion are found all around the sky, because the Sun happens to sit inside the scattered outskirts of the group, and Sirius is often counted among them, though that claim is debated. Only the core still gathers in the Dipper, a handful of bright stars that have stayed close enough to look like a pattern.

HR4295.question: Which of the Big Dipper's stars are Merak's true siblings?
HR4295.why: Merak, the lower pointer of the Big Dipper, belongs to a family that no longer looks like one: its siblings are spread across the whole pattern.
HR4295.look: Sweep from Merak across the bowl to Phecda and Megrez and out along the handle to Alioth and Mizar. All five are white and of similar brightness, a family resemblance; Dubhe, the upper pointer just five degrees from Merak, is yellow-orange.
HR4295.answer: Its true siblings are Phecda, Megrez, Alioth and Mizar with Alcor: together with Merak they drift across the sky at the same rate in the same direction, the signature of a shared birth about 414 million years ago. Dubhe and Alkaid, the two ends of the Dipper, are passers-by, and Dubhe lies half again as far away as Merak.
HR4295.story: The five Dipper siblings are no longer bound to one another, but they set out with nearly the same velocity, and small differences in speed take hundreds of millions of years to pull siblings far apart. Over the next hundred thousand years or so the Dipper's outline will warp, as Dubhe and Alkaid go their own ways, while these five keep traveling together.

NGC6871.beat: Scattered: a family that kept its dead
NGC6871.question: Do the siblings of a dead star keep traveling with what it left behind?
NGC6871.why: NGC 6871 is the bright core of a loose association of hot young stars in Cygnus, a family already spreading out, and one of its members has already reached the end of its life.
NGC6871.look: From η Cygni in the swan's neck, move about two degrees east-north-east to a compact scatter of fairly bright white stars. Sweep around it at low power to sense the wider spread of bright stars that belong to the same family.
NGC6871.answer: The siblings and the remains travel on together: Cygnus X-1, very likely the black hole left by one of the family's heaviest members, still moves with the young stars of NGC 6871 to within about 9 km/s. A family's shared motion outlasts even the death of its members, which is why it is the last tie astronomers can follow.
NGC6871.story: Following a black hole through space is possible only because it has a visible partner. The blue supergiant it orbits can be tracked like any star. Its parallax and drift across the sky are measured with radio telescopes that pick out the system's compact radio glow, and its speed along our line of sight is read from its spectrum. Put together, those motions give the system's path through the galaxy, which can then be laid beside the family's.

STAR-Antares.beat: Scattered: the red elder of Scorpius
STAR-Antares.question: Why is Antares red while its scattered siblings across Scorpius shine blue-white?
STAR-Antares.why: Antares belongs to Upper Scorpius, a family of hot young stars about 11 million years old that never formed a tight cluster, and it is the one member that has visibly moved on.
STAR-Antares.look: Put Antares near the edge of the field and let its orange-red deepen; then find σ Scorpii about two degrees west-north-west, crisp and blue-white. Two members of one family, at very different stages of life, share the view.
STAR-Antares.answer: Antares was the family's heaviest member and has aged first, the same pattern as in a cluster, only here the family is strewn across the whole Scorpion. σ Scorpii beside it and the blue-white stars of the Scorpion's head are its siblings, still in their prime, and all of them drift through space together.
STAR-Antares.story: Antares is also a clock for its family, and a contested one. Upper Scorpius was long thought to be about five million years old, until its heaviest stars, Antares among them, were found to fit an age about twice that. Newer studies suggest the family formed over a spread of several million years. A star that has already swollen into a supergiant cannot be very young, so it holds the family's age to a minimum that the small stars alone would miss.

HR5469.beat: Scattered: a branch of the Scorpius family
HR5469.question: How far across the sky do the siblings of the Scorpius stars reach?
HR5469.why: α Lupi is a hot blue-white giant in Lupus, far from any cluster, and its family is spread so widely that no single view could ever frame it.
HR5469.look: Find the clean blue-white star in a rich, scattered field south-west of Scorpius. Its color matches the bright stars of the Scorpion's head; that likeness, and a shared drift too slow to see, are all that mark it as kin.
HR5469.answer: They reach across a quarter of the southern sky. α Lupi belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, an older branch of the same great family as the Scorpius stars, now spread from Lupus to Centaurus. This is what a family looks like once nothing binds it.
HR5469.story: This scattered family may have touched the Earth. Its heaviest members have been exploding for millions of years, and the blasts are thought to have helped hollow out the bubble of thin, hot gas the Sun now sits in. Radioactive iron laid down on the deep sea floor a few million years ago is often traced to supernovae in this very group. A family can be strewn across the sky and still leave its mark on its neighbors.

HR4656.question: Are the stars of the Southern Cross a family, or only a pattern?
HR4656.why: δ Crucis, the faintest star of the Cross, belongs to a family that was born together and has since spread out over several constellations.
HR4656.look: Take in the whole Cross in one or two fields. δ Crucis, Mimosa and Acrux share a blue-white color, while Gacrux at the top glows orange; color is the one family trait you can actually see.
HR4656.answer: They are mostly a family. δ Crucis and Mimosa, and probably Acrux, share the motion of the Lower Centaurus–Crux group, while orange Gacrux is a nearer stranger that only lines up with them. The family's other members are scattered across Centaurus and beyond, still drifting the same way.
HR4656.story: The Cross's family is one branch of the largest family of young stars near the Sun, the Scorpius–Centaurus association, which stretches from Scorpius through Centaurus to Crux and holds thousands of members. Its main branches differ in age by several million years, the youngest in Scorpius, as if star birth had moved through the region in stages, and Gaia now splits even those branches into smaller groups.

HR4853.beat: Scattered: a loose sibling beside a tight family
HR4853.question: Why did Mimosa's family scatter while the Jewel Box, born at the same time, did not?
HR4853.why: Mimosa sits a degree from the Jewel Box and is about the same age, which makes this one field the clearest comparison of a family that held together and one that did not.
HR4853.look: Put Mimosa at the edge of the field and look about a degree south-east for the tight knot of the Jewel Box. Both share the same icy blue-white: one a lone sibling, the other a family still packed together.
HR4853.answer: The two families were born differently. The Jewel Box formed as a dense knot of thousands of stars whose combined gravity still holds it. Mimosa's family was born as a loose association that gravity never bound, so its members have been drifting apart from the start.
HR4853.story: Whether a birth ends in a cluster or a loose association seems to depend on how dense the gas was. Where the cloud was packed tightly, stars formed fast and close together, and their combined gravity held on after the gas cleared; where it was spread thin, the stars formed in a loose web that was never bound at all. Surveys of nearby star-forming regions find most young stars in the loose kind, which is why scattered families outnumber clusters.

HR2020.beat: Scattered: a family named for one star
HR2020.question: Why does a star only 23 million years old stand alone, with no family around it?
HR2020.why: Beta Pictoris is famous for the planet-forming disk around it, but it is also the namesake of a whole family of young stars.
HR2020.look: Sweep about six degrees west of Canopus to a lone, modest white star in an empty-looking area. Nothing in the view hints at its family, and that emptiness is the point.
HR2020.answer: It does have a family, just not a cluster: Beta Pictoris gives its name to a moving group of young stars born with it about 23 million years ago. They are now spread so widely across the sky that only their shared motion shows they belong together. Its siblings are scattered far beyond any binocular field.
HR2020.story: The family's age has been measured with two different clocks. Its faint red members still show lithium down to a sharp boundary, the same test used in clusters. The members' motions, run backward, draw together into a smaller region some twenty million years ago, and the two answers agree fairly well. As the nearest family this young, its members are among the best places to look for planets still glowing with the heat of their formation.
